Recreating Figure 1, Class 1: PCA and Bar Plots (ER-mutant dataset)

2026-10-27

Learning objectives

By the end of this tutorial you should be able to:

  1. Explain what DESeq2 is for, and name the three inputs it needs (counts matrix, sample sheet, design).
  2. Build a DESeqDataSet, explain why we filter out genes with very few reads, and run DESeq().
  3. Understand what a size factor is and why raw counts must be normalized before samples are compared.
  4. Explain what PC1 and PC2 represent, read the pcaData table, and build a PCA plot in ggplot2.
  5. Explain why biologists need to convert gene IDs, and use mapIds() with org.Hs.eg.db to turn Ensembl IDs into gene symbols.

Our goal

Over the next three classes we will recreate Figure 1 of Arnesen et al. 2021, one or two panels at a time:

Class Panel(s) Plot type
1 (today) 1A and 1C PCA plot and bar plots
2 1D Gene ontology (GO) enrichment with clusterProfiler
3 1B Heatmap with pheatmap

Open the paper and look at Figure 1A and Figure 1C. Think about:

  • 1A: What does each dot represent? What does the color tell you? What does the shape tell you? How much variance does PC1 explain?
  • 1C: What is on the y-axis? What does “relative to WT DMSO” mean? Is the y-axis linear or log scale (look at the numbers)?
  • 1C: What do the error bars and stars mean? (Read the figure legend.)

Heads-up: The paper has three ER genotypes: WT, Y537S, and D538G. Our dataset only has WT and Y537S, so our plots will have no D538G (red) samples. That’s okay. The story for Y537S is the same.

Exercises are marked with ✏️.

Step 0: The biology and the dataset (10 min)

About the dataset

Arnesen S, Blanchard Z, Williams MM, Berrett KC, Li Z, Oesterreich S, Richer JK, Gertz J. (2021). Estrogen receptor alpha mutations in breast cancer cells cause gene expression changes through constant activity and secondary effects. Cancer Res 81(3): 539–551. https://doi.org/10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-20-1171 (GEO accession: GSE148279)

Most breast cancers express estrogen receptor alpha (ER, gene name ESR1). ER is a transcription factor: when the hormone estrogen (E2) binds ER, ER moves onto the DNA and turns on genes that make the cancer cells grow. That’s why patients are treated with hormone therapies that block estrogen signaling.

About 30% of tumors that come back after hormone therapy carry a mutation in ER’s ligand-binding domain (the part that binds estrogen). The two most common are Y537S and D538G. These mutant ERs are thought to be “always on”, even without estrogen, so blocking estrogen no longer works.

The question: Does mutant ER just act like WT ER that is permanently stimulated by estrogen, or does it also turn on new genes?

The experiment: The authors used CRISPR to put the Y537S mutation into the cells’ own ESR1 gene in T-47D cells, a widely used ER-positive breast cancer cell line. Cells were grown without hormones, then treated with E2 or vehicle (DMSO, labelled veh in our files) before RNA-seq.

  • 2 genotypes: WT and Y537S (YS)
  • 2 treatments: E2 and vehicle (veh)
  • 3 replicates per group → 12 samples

Where did our data come from?

Before today, each of the 12 samples went through the RNA-seq pipeline below. The first three steps happen at the bench. Step 4 (matching each read to the gene it came from, then counting) is run on a computer cluster and takes hours, so we give you its output: a counts matrix.

A read is a short piece of sequence (here ~50–150 letters) from one RNA molecule. If a gene is strongly expressed, there are many copies of its mRNA in the cell, so it produces many reads. The number of reads for a gene is our measure of how much that gene is expressed.

We will use two files today:

File What it contains One row =
ER_mut_RNAseq_counts_matrix.csv Raw read counts for every gene in every sample one gene
sample_annotations.csv The sample sheet (metadata): which sample is which one sample

Load the required libraries

#BiocManager::install(c("DESeq2", "org.Hs.eg.db")) #if you need to install

library(DESeq2)
library(org.Hs.eg.db)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)
library(ggplot2)

Packages only need to be installed once. After that, library() is enough.

Step 1: DESeq2, from counts to a DESeqDataSet (20 min)

1a. What is DESeq2, and why do we need it?

Our main question is simple: which genes change between two groups (for example, WT cells + E2 vs WT cells + DMSO)? You might think we could just compare the read counts. Unfortunately, three problems get in the way:

Problem Example What DESeq2 does about it
Samples were sequenced to different depths WT_E2_1 has ~67 million reads, WT_veh_1 only ~46 million. Every gene looks “higher” in WT_E2_1. Calculates a size factor for each sample and divides by it (normalization)
Replicates never agree perfectly The 3 WT_veh samples give 1,619, 2,279 and 2,054 reads for the same gene. Measures how noisy each gene is (its dispersion) and asks whether the difference between groups is bigger than that noise
We test ~20,000 genes at once With p < 0.05, about 1,000 genes would look “significant” by pure chance. Reports an adjusted p-value (padj) that corrects for multiple testing

DESeq2 is an R package (from the Bioconductor project for biology software) that solves all three problems. It is one of the most widely used tools for finding differentially expressed genes in RNA-seq data. For every gene it reports:

  • log2FoldChange: how much the gene changed (log2 of group A ÷ group B)
  • pvalue and padj: how confident we are that the change is real

Today we’ll use DESeq2 for normalized counts (for the bar plots), a transformation for the PCA, and the results tables we’ll need in Classes 2 and 3.

1b. What DESeq2 needs: the three inputs

Every DESeq2 analysis starts by packing three things into one R object called a DESeqDataSet (we’ll call ours dds):

Input Argument name What it is Rules
① Counts matrix countData Number of reads for each gene (rows) in each sample (columns) Must be raw, whole-number counts. Never give DESeq2 normalized values (TPM, FPKM, log counts), because it does its own normalization.
② Sample sheet colData One row per sample, describing it (genotype, treatment, replicate…) Rows must be in the same order as the columns of ①
③ Design design A formula telling DESeq2 which column of ② defines the groups to compare Written with a ~, e.g. ~ group

Why is ② called colData? Because it describes the columns of the counts matrix (the samples).

1c. Read in the counts matrix

row.names = 1 makes the first column (the gene IDs) the row names, so the matrix itself contains only numbers. as.matrix() turns the table into a numeric matrix, which is what DESeq2 expects.

countdata <- read.csv("ER_mut_RNAseq_counts_matrix.csv",
                      header = TRUE,
                      row.names = 1)

countdata <- as.matrix(countdata)
dim(countdata)
## [1] 60708    12
head(countdata, 3)
##                    WT_E2_1 WT_E2_2 WT_E2_3 WT_veh_1 WT_veh_2 WT_veh_3 YS_E2_1
## ENSG00000000003.15    2509    1807    1894     1619     2279     2054    1941
## ENSG00000000005.6        0       0       0        0        0        0       0
## ENSG00000000419.14    8661    6075    6269     4886     6195     6062    7022
##                    YS_E2_2 YS_E2_3 YS_veh_1 YS_veh_2 YS_veh_3
## ENSG00000000003.15    1598    1894     1475     2210     1552
## ENSG00000000005.6        0       0        0        0        0
## ENSG00000000419.14    5791    6690     5546     7740     5711

dim() tells us there are 60708 genes (rows) and 12 samples (columns). The gene IDs look like ENSG00000000003.15: these are Ensembl IDs, a computer-friendly name for each gene. We’ll turn them into normal gene names in Step 3.

Question: Why are all of the numbers whole numbers? (Hint: what is being counted?)

1d. Read in the sample sheet

sampleTable <- read.csv("sample_annotations.csv",
                        header = TRUE)
sampleTable
##      sample ER_status condition rep  group
## 1   WT_E2_1        WT        E2   1  WT_E2
## 2   WT_E2_2        WT        E2   2  WT_E2
## 3   WT_E2_3        WT        E2   3  WT_E2
## 4  WT_veh_1        WT       veh   1 WT_veh
## 5  WT_veh_2        WT       veh   2 WT_veh
## 6  WT_veh_3        WT       veh   3 WT_veh
## 7   YS_E2_1        YS        E2   1  YS_E2
## 8   YS_E2_2        YS        E2   2  YS_E2
## 9   YS_E2_3        YS        E2   3  YS_E2
## 10 YS_veh_1        YS       veh   1 YS_veh
## 11 YS_veh_2        YS       veh   2 YS_veh
## 12 YS_veh_3        YS       veh   3 YS_veh
Column What it describes Example
sample The sample name. Must match the column names of the counts matrix WT_E2_1
ER_status ER genotype WT or YS (Y537S)
condition Treatment E2 or veh (DMSO)
rep Replicate number within the group 1, 2, 3
group Genotype + treatment combined WT_E2, WT_veh, YS_E2, YS_veh

Now the golden rule: the columns of the counts matrix must be in the same order as the rows of the sample sheet. DESeq2 does not check this by name. It simply assumes column 1 of the counts is row 1 of the sample sheet. If they were shuffled, DESeq2 would happily give you wrong answers. So always check:

all(colnames(countdata) == sampleTable$sample)
## [1] TRUE

colnames(countdata) == sampleTable$sample compares the two lists name by name (12 TRUE/FALSE values), and all() asks “are they all TRUE?”. If you ever get FALSE, reorder the counts to match: countdata <- countdata[, sampleTable$sample].

1e. Build the DESeqDataSet

This is one of the most important steps in the whole analysis: everything after it (normalization, statistics, PCA, the results tables for Classes 2 and 3) is calculated from this one object. The function is DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(), and it takes exactly the three inputs from the diagram above:

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = countdata,
                              colData = sampleTable,
                              design = ~ group)

What each part means:

Code Meaning
countData = countdata ① The raw counts matrix we read in 1c
colData = sampleTable ② The sample sheet we read in 1d
design = ~ group ③ “Gene expression is explained by group”. Each of the four combinations (WT_veh, WT_E2, YS_veh, YS_E2) is its own group, so later we can compare any two of them

If you run this yourself you’ll see a warning: “some variables in design formula are characters, converting to factors”. That’s fine. DESeq2 is telling you it turned the text in the group column into a factor (R’s word for a categorical variable).

Let’s look at what we built:

dds
## class: DESeqDataSet 
## dim: 60708 12 
## metadata(1): version
## assays(1): counts
## rownames(60708): ENSG00000000003.15 ENSG00000000005.6 ...
##   ENSG00000288724.1 ENSG00000288725.1
## rowData names(0):
## colnames(12): WT_E2_1 WT_E2_2 ... YS_veh_2 YS_veh_3
## colData names(5): sample ER_status condition rep group

How to read this summary:

Line What it tells us
class: DESeqDataSet The type of object
dim: 60708 12 60708 genes × 12 samples
assays(1): counts The counts matrix is stored inside. Get it back with counts(dds)
rownames(60708): ENSG... The gene IDs
colnames(12): WT_E2_1 ... The sample names
colData names(5): sample ER_status ... The sample sheet is stored inside. Get it back with colData(dds)

dds is like a folder that keeps the counts and the sample information together, so they can never get out of sync. As we run more steps, DESeq2 adds more information to this same folder.

1f. Remove genes with (almost) no reads

Our matrix contains every human gene, about 60,000 of them. But a T-47D breast cancer cell doesn’t use most of them. For example, the hemoglobin gene HBB (red blood cells) and insulin INS (pancreas) have 0 reads in all 12 samples. How many genes are like this?

total_reads_per_gene <- rowSums(counts(dds))   # add up each gene's reads across all 12 samples

sum(total_reads_per_gene == 0)   # genes with no reads at all
## [1] 30257
sum(total_reads_per_gene < 10)   # genes with fewer than 10 reads in total
## [1] 37233

30257 genes (about half!) have no reads at all.

Let’s look at the whole distribution.

Each bar counts how many genes have a given total number of reads (log scale):

ggplot(data.frame(total = total_reads_per_gene),
       aes(x = log10(total + 1))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "grey60", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = log10(10 + 1), linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  annotate("text", x = log10(11) + 0.1, y = Inf, vjust = 1.5, hjust = 0,
           label = "cutoff: 10 reads", colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "log10(total reads across 12 samples + 1)",
       y = "Number of genes",
       title = "Most genes have either no reads or many reads") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = rel(1.1), hjust = 0.5))

(We add 1 before taking the log because log10(0) is undefined.) The tall bar on the left is all the genes with 0 reads.

Why do we filter out these low-count genes?

  1. They carry no information. A gene with 0, 2 or 5 reads across 12 samples can’t show a reliable difference between groups. Is 0 vs 2 reads a “change”? We can’t tell.

  2. Fewer tests = a smaller multiple-testing penalty. padj gets stricter the more genes we test. Testing ~37,000 genes that can’t be significant anyway makes it harder for the real ones to pass.

  3. Speed and memory. DESeq2 runs faster on a smaller object.

The cutoff of at least 10 reads in total is a common rule of thumb from the DESeq2 manual. It is deliberately gentle: it only removes genes that are essentially “off”.

keep <- rowSums(counts(dds)) >= 10   # TRUE for genes with 10 or more reads in total
table(keep)                          # how many genes are FALSE (removed) and TRUE (kept)?
## keep
## FALSE  TRUE 
## 37233 23475
dds <- dds[keep, ]                   # keep only the TRUE rows (genes), all columns (samples)
nrow(dds)
## [1] 23475

Reading dds[keep, ]: the part before the comma picks rows (genes), and the part after the comma picks columns (samples). Leaving it empty means “all of them”. We went from 60708 to 23475 genes.

1g. Run DESeq()

Now one command does all of the statistics:

dds <- DESeq(dds)
## estimating size factors
## estimating dispersions
## gene-wise dispersion estimates
## mean-dispersion relationship
## final dispersion estimates
## fitting model and testing

The messages DESeq2 prints match the three steps in the diagram:

Message Step
estimating size factors 1. Correct for sequencing depth
estimating dispersions, gene-wise dispersion estimates, mean-dispersion relationship, final dispersion estimates 2. Measure how noisy each gene is between replicates
fitting model and testing 3. Test every gene for a difference between groups

We’ll pull the test results out with results() in Step 5.

First, let’s look at step 1 more closely.

1h. Size factors

DESeq() stored one size factor per sample inside dds. Let’s put them next to the total number of reads in each sample:

size_factor_table <- data.frame(sample = colnames(dds),
                                total_reads = colSums(counts(dds)),
                                sizeFactor = round(sizeFactors(dds), 2))
size_factor_table
##            sample total_reads sizeFactor
## WT_E2_1   WT_E2_1    67293354       1.21
## WT_E2_2   WT_E2_2    50114317       0.89
## WT_E2_3   WT_E2_3    54970966       0.99
## WT_veh_1 WT_veh_1    46109912       0.85
## WT_veh_2 WT_veh_2    57642595       1.07
## WT_veh_3 WT_veh_3    54527318       1.01
## YS_E2_1   YS_E2_1    66020951       1.17
## YS_E2_2   YS_E2_2    51806586       0.91
## YS_E2_3   YS_E2_3    60586626       1.07
## YS_veh_1 YS_veh_1    52028633       0.91
## YS_veh_2 YS_veh_2    68631069       1.21
## YS_veh_3 YS_veh_3    51905560       0.92
Column Meaning
total_reads How many reads this sample got (its sequencing depth)
sizeFactor How much bigger (> 1) or smaller (< 1) this sample is than a typical sample

Samples with more reads get bigger size factors. Normalized count = raw count ÷ size factor, which puts all samples on the same scale. We’ll use the normalized counts for the bar plots (counts(dds, normalized = TRUE)).

Question: Which sample has the biggest size factor? Does it also have the most reads? The match is close but not perfect. DESeq2 doesn’t just use the total reads; it uses a method called median of ratios, which ignores a few extremely highly expressed genes that could otherwise skew the total.

Question: We used design = ~ group. The group column has four levels (WT_E2, WT_veh, YS_E2, YS_veh). Why is this handy when we want to compare any two of the four groups?

Step 2: The PCA plot, Figure 1A (12 min)

2a. What is PCA?

Each sample has an expression value for ~23,000 genes. We can’t draw a graph with 23,000 axes, so how do we see which samples look alike? Principal component analysis (PCA) squeezes all of those genes into a few new axes called principal components (PCs). The idea is easiest to see with just 2 genes:

  • PC1 is the direction in which the samples are most different from each other. It is the single most important pattern in the data.
  • PC2 is the second biggest pattern, at a right angle to PC1 (it captures a different difference).
  • Each PC comes with a percent of variance explained: how much of the total difference between samples it captures. If PC1 explains 90%, almost all the differences between samples are along PC1.
  • A PC1 vs PC2 plot therefore shows the two biggest patterns in the data. Samples close together have similar expression; samples far apart are different. Each dot is one sample, not one gene.

2b. Transform the counts first

Before PCA we transform the counts with vst() (variance stabilizing transformation). Raw counts span from 0 to hundreds of thousands, so a few very highly expressed genes would dominate the PCA. vst() puts the counts on a log2-like scale so that every gene has a fair say. It also uses the size factors, so differences in sequencing depth are removed.

vsd <- vst(dds, blind = FALSE)

2c. The pcaData table

DESeq2 has a built-in plotPCA(). With returnData = TRUE it gives us the numbers instead of a plot, so we can build the plot ourselves in ggplot2. intgroup (“interesting groups”) lists the sample sheet columns we want to use for coloring.

pcaData <- plotPCA(vsd,
                   intgroup = c("ER_status", "condition"),
                   returnData = TRUE)
pcaData
##                 PC1        PC2  group     name   sample ER_status condition rep
## WT_E2_1   -7.634018 -5.4179196  WT:E2  WT_E2_1  WT_E2_1        WT        E2   1
## WT_E2_2   -8.598001 -5.1410303  WT:E2  WT_E2_2  WT_E2_2        WT        E2   2
## WT_E2_3   -8.344029 -4.9307856  WT:E2  WT_E2_3  WT_E2_3        WT        E2   3
## WT_veh_1 -13.768994  4.0628972 WT:veh WT_veh_1 WT_veh_1        WT       veh   1
## WT_veh_2 -13.768525  4.1046262 WT:veh WT_veh_2 WT_veh_2        WT       veh   2
## WT_veh_3 -13.922712  3.7948229 WT:veh WT_veh_3 WT_veh_3        WT       veh   3
## YS_E2_1   10.880103  0.5362489  YS:E2  YS_E2_1  YS_E2_1        YS        E2   1
## YS_E2_2   10.968972  0.7092297  YS:E2  YS_E2_2  YS_E2_2        YS        E2   2
## YS_E2_3   11.168537  0.3609225  YS:E2  YS_E2_3  YS_E2_3        YS        E2   3
## YS_veh_1  11.132128  0.2658711 YS:veh YS_veh_1 YS_veh_1        YS       veh   1
## YS_veh_2  11.212148  0.5823619 YS:veh YS_veh_2 YS_veh_2        YS       veh   2
## YS_veh_3  10.674391  1.0727550 YS:veh YS_veh_3 YS_veh_3        YS       veh   3
##          group.1 sizeFactor
## WT_E2_1    WT_E2  1.2124403
## WT_E2_2    WT_E2  0.8907586
## WT_E2_3    WT_E2  0.9892323
## WT_veh_1  WT_veh  0.8475174
## WT_veh_2  WT_veh  1.0689202
## WT_veh_3  WT_veh  1.0074278
## YS_E2_1    YS_E2  1.1726893
## YS_E2_2    YS_E2  0.9147983
## YS_E2_3    YS_E2  1.0678230
## YS_veh_1  YS_veh  0.9091385
## YS_veh_2  YS_veh  1.2103246
## YS_veh_3  YS_veh  0.9161154

If you run this yourself, you’ll see the message “using ntop=500 top features by variance”. plotPCA() uses the 500 genes that vary most between samples, because genes that are the same in every sample can’t help tell samples apart.

Column What it is Where it came from
PC1 The sample’s position on the x-axis (its score on PC1) Calculated by PCA
PC2 The sample’s position on the y-axis (its score on PC2) Calculated by PCA
group ER_status and condition pasted together (e.g. WT:E2) Made by plotPCA() from intgroup. Careful: this replaces our own group column
name The sample name Column names of vsd
sample, ER_status, condition, rep Copied from the sample sheet colData(dds), from Step 1d
group.1 Our original group column (e.g. WT_E2), renamed because plotPCA() already used the name group Sample sheet
sizeFactor Each sample’s size factor Added by DESeq() in Step 1h. It is not used in the PCA plot, it’s just carried along with the sample information

(Older versions of DESeq2 only return PC1, PC2, group, the intgroup columns and name. If your table has fewer columns, that’s why.)

What do the PC1 and PC2 numbers mean? The numbers themselves have no units; what matters is which samples are close together and which are far apart. Let’s average the scores for each of the four groups:

pcaData |>
  dplyr::group_by(ER_status, condition) |>
  dplyr::summarise(mean_PC1 = round(mean(PC1), 1),
                   mean_PC2 = round(mean(PC2), 1),
                   .groups = "drop")
## # A tibble: 4 × 4
##   ER_status condition mean_PC1 mean_PC2
##   <chr>     <chr>        <dbl>    <dbl>
## 1 WT        E2            -8.2     -5.2
## 2 WT        veh          -13.8      4  
## 3 YS        E2            11        0.5
## 4 YS        veh           11        0.6
  • PC1 splits WT (negative) from Y537S (positive). The biggest difference in the whole experiment is the genotype.
  • PC2 splits WT + E2 from WT + DMSO, but the two Y537S groups sit in the same place. The second biggest difference is the E2 response of WT cells.
  • The sign (+ or −) of a PC is arbitrary. If your PC1 values are flipped, the plot is mirrored but means the same thing.

The axis labels in Figure 1A show the percent of variance each PC explains. plotPCA() stores this in an attribute (a hidden note attached to pcaData):

percentVar <- round(100 * attr(pcaData, "percentVar"))
percentVar
## [1] 90  8

PC1 explains 90% of the variation between samples, and PC2 explains 8%.

2d. Build the plot

✏️ Exercise 2.1 — Which columns go where? In Figure 1A, color shows the ESR1 status and shape shows the treatment. Fill in the blanks with column names from pcaData.

ggplot(pcaData, aes(x = ___, y = ___, color = ___, shape = ___)) +
  geom_point(size = 4)
Show solution 
ggplot(pcaData, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = ER_status, shape = condition)) +
  geom_point(size = 4)

Now let’s make it look like Figure 1A, one change at a time:

  • WT in blue, Y537S in orange (scale_color_manual)
  • DMSO as squares (shape 15), E2 as circles (shape 16) (scale_shape_manual)
  • Axis labels with the percent variance (paste0 pastes text and numbers together)
pca_plot <- ggplot(pcaData, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = ER_status, shape = condition)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  scale_color_manual(name = "ESR1 status",
                     values = c(WT = "steelblue", YS = "darkorange"),
                     labels = c(WT = "WT", YS = "Y537S")) +
  scale_shape_manual(name = "Treatment",
                     values = c(veh = 15, E2 = 16),
                     labels = c(veh = "DMSO", E2 = "E2"),
                     breaks = c("veh", "E2")) +
  labs(title = "PCA of RNA-seq: WT vs Y537S",
       x = paste0("PC1 (", percentVar[1], "%)"),
       y = paste0("PC2 (", percentVar[2], "%)")) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = rel(1.2), hjust = 0.5))

pca_plot

Question: Which variable separates samples along PC1: genotype or treatment? Look at the Y537S samples: do the E2 circles and DMSO squares separate? What does that tell you about whether the mutant ER needs estrogen?

✏️ Exercise 2.2 (if you have time) — Change the column, change the story. Change color = ER_status to color = condition and shape = condition to shape = ER_status (you’ll also need to remove the two scale_..._manual() lines). Does the plot say anything different? Which version makes the main finding easier to see?

Show solution 
ggplot(pcaData, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = condition, shape = ER_status)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  theme_classic()

The dots are in exactly the same places; only the color and shape changed. Coloring by genotype makes the big PC1 split jump out, which is the main finding of Figure 1A. The plot doesn’t change, but what the reader notices first does.

Step 3: Gene ID conversion, finding our genes (10 min)

Figure 1C shows two genes:

  • CISH: a classic E2-regulated gene. The authors call it ligand-independent because it is “on” in mutant cells even without E2.
  • CASC5: a mutant-specific gene. It changes in mutant cells but does not respond to E2 in WT cells.

But our counts matrix doesn’t contain the words “CISH” or “CASC5”. It only has IDs like ENSG00000114737.16. Before we can find our genes, we need to convert gene IDs.

3a. Why gene ID conversion is a skill every biologist needs

Every gene has several names, given by different databases:

ID type Example (CISH) Who makes it Where you’ll meet it
Ensembl gene ID ENSG00000114737 Ensembl (EMBL-EBI, Europe) Output of most RNA-seq pipelines, like our counts file
Entrez (NCBI) Gene ID 1154 NCBI (USA) KEGG pathways, many enrichment tools
Gene symbol CISH HGNC, the official human gene naming committee Papers, figures, conversations, qPCR primer orders
Aliases CIS, SOCS, G18 Older papers, other labs Old literature; may point to the wrong gene

Why it matters:

  • Computers and people use different names. Pipelines use Ensembl IDs because they never change meaning and are unique. People use symbols because they are short and memorable. To go from a results table to a figure or a paper, you have to convert.
  • Different tools want different IDs. In Class 2, GO enrichment needs IDs the GO database understands. KEGG wants Entrez IDs. Getting this wrong is one of the most common reasons an analysis “finds nothing”.
  • Gene names change. CASC5 was officially renamed KNL1, and searching an up-to-date table for “CASC5” finds nothing. A famous example: Excel silently turned gene names like SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates (2-Sep, 1-Mar) in thousands of published supplementary files. In 2020 these genes were officially renamed SEPTIN2 and MARCHF1 to stop this from happening.
  • Not every ID has a match. Many Ensembl genes (new non-coding RNAs, pseudogenes) don’t have an official symbol yet, so some conversions will come back empty (NA).

3b. The tools we use in this step

To be completely clear about which program does what:

Tool What kind of thing it is What it does here
sub() A base R function (comes with R) Removes the version number (.16) from each Ensembl ID
org.Hs.eg.db A Bioconductor annotation package: a database file installed on your computer. Hs = Homo sapiens, eg = Entrez Gene The dictionary: a big table that links Ensembl IDs, Entrez IDs, symbols, aliases, gene names… for every human gene. There are matching packages for other species, e.g. org.Mm.eg.db for mouse
AnnotationDbi A Bioconductor package that is loaded automatically with org.Hs.eg.db Provides the functions that look things up in the dictionary: keytypes(), mapIds() and select()
mapIds() A function from AnnotationDbi Converts a list of IDs of one type into another type, one answer per ID

Because org.Hs.eg.db lives on your computer, the lookup works offline and is fast. It is updated twice a year, so a newer version may know about newer gene names. (Other ways to convert IDs that you may meet: the biomaRt R package and the Ensembl BioMart website, which query Ensembl online, and the g:Profiler g:Convert web tool.)

What kinds of IDs does our dictionary know about? keytypes() lists them:

keytypes(org.Hs.eg.db)
##  [1] "ACCNUM"       "ALIAS"        "ENSEMBL"      "ENSEMBLPROT"  "ENSEMBLTRANS"
##  [6] "ENTREZID"     "ENZYME"       "EVIDENCE"     "EVIDENCEALL"  "GENENAME"    
## [11] "GENETYPE"     "GO"           "GOALL"        "IPI"          "MAP"         
## [16] "OMIM"         "ONTOLOGY"     "ONTOLOGYALL"  "PATH"         "PFAM"        
## [21] "PMID"         "PROSITE"      "REFSEQ"       "SYMBOL"       "UCSCKG"      
## [26] "UNIPROT"

We have ENSEMBL IDs and we want SYMBOLs. Both are in the list, so we’re good.

Watch out: AnnotationDbi has a function called select(), and so does dplyr. Whichever package was loaded last “wins” (R calls this masking). This is why this tutorial always writes dplyr::select() and dplyr::filter(): the dplyr:: tells R exactly which package’s function to use.

3c. Remove the version number

Our IDs have a version number at the end (ENSG00000114737.16). The version goes up each time Ensembl updates the gene’s structure. The dictionary stores IDs without the version, so we need to drop it. sub("\\..*", "", x) means “replace the first dot and everything after it with nothing”.

ensembl_ids <- sub("\\..*", "", rownames(dds))
head(rownames(dds), 3)
## [1] "ENSG00000000003.15" "ENSG00000000419.14" "ENSG00000000457.14"
head(ensembl_ids, 3)
## [1] "ENSG00000000003" "ENSG00000000419" "ENSG00000000457"

3d. Look up the gene symbols with mapIds()

symbols <- mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db,         # the dictionary to look in
                  keys = ensembl_ids,   # the IDs we have
                  keytype = "ENSEMBL",  # what kind of IDs they are
                  column = "SYMBOL")    # what kind of ID we want back
head(symbols)
## ENSG00000000003 ENSG00000000419 ENSG00000000457 ENSG00000000460 ENSG00000000938 
##        "TSPAN6"          "DPM1"         "SCYL3"         "FIRRM"           "FGR" 
## ENSG00000000971 
##           "CFH"
Argument Our value Meaning
first argument org.Hs.eg.db Which dictionary (species) to use
keys ensembl_ids The list of IDs to convert. Here, all 23475 of our genes
keytype "ENSEMBL" The type of ID in keys (what we have)
column "SYMBOL" The type of ID to return (what we want)

How many genes didn’t get a symbol?

sum(is.na(symbols))
## [1] 5243

5243 of our 23475 genes have no symbol (NA). Most of these are non-coding RNAs or pseudogenes. We keep them in the data; they just won’t have a name.

3e. A table of normalized counts with symbols

Let’s put the normalized counts (raw counts ÷ size factor, from Step 1h) and the symbols into one table:

norm_counts <- as.data.frame(counts(dds, normalized = TRUE)) |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("ensembl_id_version") |>
  dplyr::mutate(ensembl_id = ensembl_ids,
                symbol = symbols,
                .after = ensembl_id_version)

head(norm_counts, 3)
##   ensembl_id_version      ensembl_id symbol  WT_E2_1  WT_E2_2  WT_E2_3 WT_veh_1
## 1 ENSG00000000003.15 ENSG00000000003 TSPAN6 2069.380 2028.608 1914.616 1910.285
## 2 ENSG00000000419.14 ENSG00000000419   DPM1 7143.445 6820.030 6337.237 5765.073
## 3 ENSG00000000457.14 ENSG00000000457  SCYL3 1631.421 1703.043 1527.447 1850.110
##   WT_veh_2 WT_veh_3  YS_E2_1  YS_E2_2  YS_E2_3 YS_veh_1 YS_veh_2 YS_veh_3
## 1 2132.058 2038.856 1655.170 1746.833 1773.702 1622.415 1825.956 1694.110
## 2 5795.568 6017.305 5987.946 6330.357 6265.083 6100.281 6394.979 6233.931
## 3 1842.981 1950.512 1494.002 1402.495 1455.297 1479.423 1557.433 1545.657

✏️ Exercise 3.1 — Where is CASC5? Use dplyr::filter() to find the rows for "CISH" and "CASC5". How many rows do you get?

norm_counts |>
  dplyr::filter(symbol %in% c("___", "___"))
Show solution 
norm_counts |>
  dplyr::filter(symbol %in% c("CISH", "CASC5"))
##   ensembl_id_version      ensembl_id symbol  WT_E2_1  WT_E2_2  WT_E2_3 WT_veh_1
## 1 ENSG00000114737.16 ENSG00000114737   CISH 1330.375 1504.336 1612.361 503.8245
##   WT_veh_2 WT_veh_3  YS_E2_1  YS_E2_2 YS_E2_3 YS_veh_1 YS_veh_2 YS_veh_3
## 1 473.3749 525.0997 1657.728 1480.108 1699.72 1571.818 1459.939 1691.927

Only one row: CISH. CASC5 is missing because the gene has been renamed.

So what is CASC5 called now? The dictionary also stores old names as ALIAS. We can use mapIds() the other way around: from alias to official symbol:

mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db,
       keys = "CASC5",
       keytype = "ALIAS",
       column = "SYMBOL")
##  CASC5 
## "KNL1"

CASC5’s official symbol is now KNL1 (kinetochore scaffold 1). You can also look up a gene on genecards.org or ensembl.org. Searching by its Ensembl ID is the safest, because IDs don’t change when names do.

We’ll use the current name, KNL1, and remember that it is called CASC5 in the paper:

genes_fig1c <- c("CISH", "KNL1")

norm_counts |>
  dplyr::filter(symbol %in% genes_fig1c)
##   ensembl_id_version      ensembl_id symbol  WT_E2_1  WT_E2_2  WT_E2_3
## 1 ENSG00000114737.16 ENSG00000114737   CISH 1330.375 1504.336 1612.361
## 2 ENSG00000137812.20 ENSG00000137812   KNL1 2095.773 1515.562 1788.255
##    WT_veh_1  WT_veh_2  WT_veh_3  YS_E2_1  YS_E2_2  YS_E2_3 YS_veh_1 YS_veh_2
## 1  503.8245  473.3749  525.0997 1657.728 1480.108 1699.720 1571.818 1459.939
## 2 1818.2518 1859.8208 1763.8981 3595.155 3864.240 3925.744 3650.709 3744.450
##   YS_veh_3
## 1 1691.927
## 2 3762.626

Step 4: The bar plots, Figure 1C (18 min)

4a. From wide to long format

norm_counts is in wide format: one row per gene, one column per sample. ggplot2 likes long format: one row per gene per sample. pivot_longer() does this, and left_join() adds the sample sheet information (genotype, treatment, group) to every row.

fig1c_long <- norm_counts |>
  dplyr::filter(symbol %in% genes_fig1c) |>
  dplyr::select(-ensembl_id_version, -ensembl_id) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = -symbol,
                      names_to = "sample",
                      values_to = "norm_count") |>
  dplyr::left_join(sampleTable, by = "sample")

fig1c_long
## # A tibble: 24 × 7
##    symbol sample   norm_count ER_status condition   rep group 
##    <chr>  <chr>         <dbl> <chr>     <chr>     <int> <chr> 
##  1 CISH   WT_E2_1       1330. WT        E2            1 WT_E2 
##  2 CISH   WT_E2_2       1504. WT        E2            2 WT_E2 
##  3 CISH   WT_E2_3       1612. WT        E2            3 WT_E2 
##  4 CISH   WT_veh_1       504. WT        veh           1 WT_veh
##  5 CISH   WT_veh_2       473. WT        veh           2 WT_veh
##  6 CISH   WT_veh_3       525. WT        veh           3 WT_veh
##  7 CISH   YS_E2_1       1658. YS        E2            1 YS_E2 
##  8 CISH   YS_E2_2       1480. YS        E2            2 YS_E2 
##  9 CISH   YS_E2_3       1700. YS        E2            3 YS_E2 
## 10 CISH   YS_veh_1      1572. YS        veh           1 YS_veh
## # ℹ 14 more rows

4b. Relative expression

Figure 1C shows expression relative to WT DMSO: for each gene, the average of the WT vehicle samples is set to 1, and every other sample is divided by that average. A value of 2 means “twice as much as WT DMSO”.

✏️ Exercise 4.1 — Pick the reference group. Fill in the blank with the group that everything should be relative to.

fig1c_long <- fig1c_long |>
  dplyr::group_by(symbol) |>
  dplyr::mutate(rel_expr = norm_count / mean(norm_count[group == "___"])) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()
Show solution 
fig1c_long <- fig1c_long |>
  dplyr::group_by(symbol) |>
  dplyr::mutate(rel_expr = norm_count / mean(norm_count[group == "WT_veh"])) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()

group_by(symbol) makes sure each gene is divided by its own WT DMSO average.

Check: the three WT_veh samples should now average to exactly 1 for each gene.

fig1c_long |>
  dplyr::filter(group == "WT_veh") |>
  dplyr::group_by(symbol) |>
  dplyr::summarise(mean_rel = mean(rel_expr))
## # A tibble: 2 × 2
##   symbol mean_rel
##   <chr>     <dbl>
## 1 CISH          1
## 2 KNL1          1

4c. Mean ± SEM

Each bar is the mean of 3 replicates, and the error bar is the standard error of the mean (SEM) = standard deviation / √n.

fig1c_summary <- fig1c_long |>
  dplyr::group_by(symbol, group, ER_status, condition) |>
  dplyr::summarise(mean_rel = mean(rel_expr),
                   sem_rel = sd(rel_expr) / sqrt(n()),
                   .groups = "drop")

fig1c_summary
## # A tibble: 8 × 6
##   symbol group  ER_status condition mean_rel sem_rel
##   <chr>  <chr>  <chr>     <chr>        <dbl>   <dbl>
## 1 CISH   WT_E2  WT        E2           2.96   0.164 
## 2 CISH   WT_veh WT        veh          1      0.0300
## 3 CISH   YS_E2  YS        E2           3.22   0.134 
## 4 CISH   YS_veh YS        veh          3.14   0.134 
## 5 KNL1   WT_E2  WT        E2           0.992  0.0924
## 6 KNL1   WT_veh WT        veh          1      0.0153
## 7 KNL1   YS_E2  YS        E2           2.09   0.0560
## 8 KNL1   YS_veh YS        veh          2.05   0.0191

The paper orders bars WT DMSO, WT E2, Y537S DMSO, Y537S E2. Like last time, we use a factor to control the order (otherwise R uses alphabetical order):

group_order <- c("WT_veh", "WT_E2", "YS_veh", "YS_E2")
fig1c_long$group <- factor(fig1c_long$group, levels = group_order)
fig1c_summary$group <- factor(fig1c_summary$group, levels = group_order)

4d. Our first bar plot

✏️ Exercise 4.2 — Which columns go where? Each bar is a group, the height is the mean relative expression, and the bar color shows the genotype. Fill in the blanks.

ggplot(fig1c_summary, aes(x = ___, y = ___, fill = ___)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ symbol, scales = "free_y")
Show solution 
ggplot(fig1c_summary, aes(x = group, y = mean_rel, fill = ER_status)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ symbol, scales = "free_y")

facet_wrap(~ symbol) makes one small panel per gene. scales = "free_y" lets each gene have its own y-axis range.

4e. Polish the figure

Now we add, one layer at a time:

  • error bars (geom_errorbar) and the individual replicates (geom_point)
  • a dashed line at 1 (= same as WT DMSO)
  • WT blue / Y537S orange, and readable x-axis labels
  • italic gene names in the panel titles (strip.text)
fig1c_plot <- ggplot() +
  geom_col(data = fig1c_summary,
           aes(x = group, y = mean_rel, fill = ER_status),
           color = "black", width = 0.7) +
  geom_errorbar(data = fig1c_summary,
                aes(x = group, ymin = mean_rel - sem_rel, ymax = mean_rel + sem_rel),
                width = 0.25) +
  geom_point(data = fig1c_long,
             aes(x = group, y = rel_expr),
             size = 1.5,
             position = position_jitter(width = 0.1, seed = 1)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~ symbol, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(name = "ESR1 status",
                    values = c(WT = "steelblue", YS = "darkorange"),
                    labels = c(WT = "WT", YS = "Y537S")) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c(WT_veh = "DMSO", WT_E2 = "E2",
                              YS_veh = "DMSO", YS_E2 = "E2")) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(x = NULL,
       y = "Relative expression\n(relative to WT DMSO)") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(size = rel(1.3), face = "italic"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = rel(1.1), colour = "black"),
        legend.position = "bottom")

fig1c_plot

Question: Look at CISH. In WT cells, what does E2 do? In Y537S cells, is CISH already high without E2? This is what the authors call ligand-independent. Now look at KNL1: does E2 change it in WT cells? Why do the authors call it mutant-specific?

4f. Significance stars

The figure legend says: “Student two-sample t test was used: **, P < 0.01; ***, P < 0.001; ****, P < 0.0001; n.s., not significant.” Each bar is compared with WT DMSO.

✏️ Exercise 4.3 — One t-test by hand. Compare CISH in WT_E2 vs WT_veh. Fill in the two group names. (var.equal = TRUE makes it a classic Student’s t-test, as in the paper.)

cish <- fig1c_long |> dplyr::filter(symbol == "CISH")

t.test(cish$rel_expr[cish$group == "___"],
       cish$rel_expr[cish$group == "___"],
       var.equal = TRUE)
Show solution 
cish <- fig1c_long |> dplyr::filter(symbol == "CISH")

t.test(cish$rel_expr[cish$group == "WT_E2"],
       cish$rel_expr[cish$group == "WT_veh"],
       var.equal = TRUE)
## 
##  Two Sample t-test
## 
## data:  cish$rel_expr[cish$group == "WT_E2"] and cish$rel_expr[cish$group == "WT_veh"]
## t = 11.755, df = 4, p-value = 0.0002996
## alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  1.497215 2.423140
## sample estimates:
## mean of x mean of y 
##  2.960178  1.000000

Doing this by hand for 2 genes × 3 groups would be 6 t-tests. Instead, we let R loop over every row of the summary table with rowwise(). Inside rowwise(), symbol and group mean “the value in this row”:

fig1c_stats <- fig1c_summary |>
  dplyr::filter(group != "WT_veh") |>
  dplyr::rowwise() |>
  dplyr::mutate(p_value = t.test(
    fig1c_long$rel_expr[fig1c_long$symbol == symbol & fig1c_long$group == group],
    fig1c_long$rel_expr[fig1c_long$symbol == symbol & fig1c_long$group == "WT_veh"],
    var.equal = TRUE)$p.value,
    # tallest replicate in this group, so the star sits above every point
    ymax = max(fig1c_long$rel_expr[fig1c_long$symbol == symbol & fig1c_long$group == group])) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::mutate(label = dplyr::case_when(p_value < 0.0001 ~ "****",
                                         p_value < 0.001  ~ "***",
                                         p_value < 0.01   ~ "**",
                                         TRUE             ~ "n.s."))

fig1c_stats |> dplyr::select(symbol, group, mean_rel, p_value, label)
## # A tibble: 6 × 5
##   symbol group  mean_rel    p_value label
##   <chr>  <fct>     <dbl>      <dbl> <chr>
## 1 CISH   WT_E2     2.96  0.000300   ***  
## 2 CISH   YS_E2     3.22  0.0000866  **** 
## 3 CISH   YS_veh    3.14  0.0000975  **** 
## 4 KNL1   WT_E2     0.992 0.938      n.s. 
## 5 KNL1   YS_E2     2.09  0.0000469  **** 
## 6 KNL1   YS_veh    2.05  0.00000177 ****

Add the stars just above the tallest point in each group:

fig1c_final <- fig1c_plot +
  geom_text(data = fig1c_stats,
            aes(x = group, y = ymax * 1.08, label = label),
            size = 4.5)

fig1c_final

Step 5: Save for next class (2 min)

Next class we will run GO enrichment, and the class after that we’ll make a heatmap. Both need the DESeq2 results for two comparisons:

Comparison Question it answers
WT_E2 vs WT_veh Which genes respond to estrogen in normal (WT) cells?
YS_veh vs WT_veh Which genes are different in mutant cells, even without estrogen?

results(dds, contrast = c("group", "WT_E2", "WT_veh")) means “in the group column, compare WT_E2 (top of the fold change) with WT_veh (bottom)”. This is where design = ~ group from Step 1e pays off.

Run this chunk to save the results (copies of these files are also in the folder, in case you didn’t finish today):

save_results <- function(numerator, denominator) {
  res <- results(dds, contrast = c("group", numerator, denominator))
  res_df <- as.data.frame(res) |>
    tibble::rownames_to_column("ensembl_id_version") |>
    dplyr::mutate(ensembl_id = ensembl_ids,
                  symbol = symbols,
                  .after = ensembl_id_version)
  write.csv(res_df,
            paste0("ERmut_DESeq2_", numerator, "_vs_", denominator, ".csv"),
            row.names = FALSE)
  res_df
}

res_E2 <- save_results("WT_E2", "WT_veh")
res_YS <- save_results("YS_veh", "WT_veh")

write.csv(norm_counts, "ERmut_normalized_counts.csv", row.names = FALSE)

Save today’s figures:

ggsave("Fig1A_PCA_WT_vs_Y537S.png", pca_plot, width = 6, height = 4.5)
ggsave("Fig1C_barplots_CISH_KNL1.png", fig1c_final, width = 7, height = 4.5)

Step 6: On your own: GREB1 (finish at home if needed)

GREB1 (growth regulating estrogen receptor binding 1) is one of the best-known estrogen-responsive genes in breast cancer. ER binds right next to it, and labs often measure GREB1 by qPCR as a quick read-out of “is ER active?”. It isn’t in Figure 1C, so you will make its bar plot yourself, in the same style, and decide which category it belongs to.

Your task: make a Figure 1C-style bar plot for GREB1 (relative to WT DMSO, mean ± SEM, individual replicates, t-test stars vs WT DMSO), save it, and interpret it.

Everything you need is in Step 4. Work through the checklist below. Each step has a fill-in chunk and a hidden solution. Try on your own first! Use new object names starting with greb1_ so you don’t overwrite the CISH/KNL1 objects.

Before you start, predict: Will GREB1 go up with E2 in WT cells? Will it be high in Y537S cells without E2?

✏️ Exercise 6.1 — Find the gene. Check that GREB1 is in norm_counts under that name. How many rows do you expect?

  dplyr::filter(symbol == "___")
Show solution

One row. GREB1 hasn’t been renamed, so no alias lookup is needed. Notice how much higher its normalized counts are in WT_E2 than in WT_veh.

  dplyr::group_by(symbol, group, ER_status, condition) |>
  dplyr::summarise(mean_rel = mean(rel_expr),
                   sem_rel = sd(rel_expr) / sqrt(n()),
                   .groups = "drop")

greb1_long$group <- factor(greb1_long$group, levels = group_order)
greb1_summary$group <- factor(greb1_summary$group, levels = group_order)

Show solution 
greb1_plot <- ggplot() +
  geom_col(data = greb1_summary,
           aes(x = group, y = mean_rel, fill = ER_status),
           color = "black", width = 0.7) +
  geom_errorbar(data = greb1_summary,
                aes(x = group, ymin = mean_rel - sem_rel, ymax = mean_rel + sem_rel),
                width = 0.25) +
  geom_point(data = greb1_long,
             aes(x = group, y = rel_expr),
             size = 1.5,
             position = position_jitter(width = 0.1, seed = 1)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~ symbol, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(name = "ESR1 status",
                    values = c(WT = "steelblue", YS = "darkorange"),
                    labels = c(WT = "WT", YS = "Y537S")) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c(WT_veh = "DMSO", WT_E2 = "E2",
                              YS_veh = "DMSO", YS_E2 = "E2")) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(x = NULL,
       y = "Relative expression\n(relative to WT DMSO)") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(size = rel(1.3), face = "italic"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = rel(1.1), colour = "black"),
        legend.position = "bottom")

Compare with Figure 1

Put your two plots next to Figures 1A and 1C and discuss:

  1. In the paper, PC1 explains 40% of the variance; in ours it explains 90%. We only have two genotypes (no D538G). Why might that make PC1 explain more of the variance?
  2. In both plots, do Y537S E2 and Y537S DMSO samples look alike? What does that say about mutant ER and estrogen?
  3. In the paper CISH goes up ~8× with E2 in WT cells; in ours it’s about 3×. Check the figure legend: what method did the authors use for Figure 1C? Why might qPCR and RNA-seq give different numbers?
  4. The paper’s error bars come from two clones per genotype; ours come from three replicates. Are those the same kind of replicate?

Key columns we used today:

File / object Column Used for
sample_annotations.csv sample matching samples to count columns
group DESeq2 design, bar order, t-tests
ER_status PCA color, bar fill
condition PCA shape
dds (after DESeq()) sizeFactor normalizing counts for sequencing depth
pcaData PC1, PC2 x- and y-axis of the PCA
norm_counts ensembl_id looking up gene symbols
symbol finding CISH, KNL1 and GREB1
fig1c_long, greb1_long rel_expr individual points, t-tests
fig1c_summary, greb1_summary mean_rel, sem_rel bar height and error bars
